MESSAGE:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a name for the delivery van
2. Work out the drop order and timeline meeting all time windows, the break and the 12:00 return  KEY: Only feasible order is B -> A -> C. Leave 08:30, arrive B 08:50, unload to 09:05 (done before 09:30); arrive A 09:30, unload to 09:45 (inside 09:00-10:00); arrive C 10:25, wait until 11:00 (take the 30-min break during this wait); unload 11:00-11:15; back at depot 12:00 exactly (zero slack). A-first fails (B reached 09:40, after opening). Must give order B, A, C with a timeline that respects all constraints.
3. Rewrite the delivery text to be friendlier
4. List three furniture checks before handover
5. Recommend paper vs emailed delivery note
6. Define 'proof of delivery' in a line
7. Draft an evening-before arrival text under 160 characters

ANSWER:
Here's everything, starting with tomorrow's route, because it only just works.

## Tomorrow's route: B → A → C

This is the only order that meets every window.
- **A first fails:** arriving at 09:00 and unloading until 09:15 puts the van at B at 09:40, after the shop opens.
- **C can't come before A or B:** C won't accept anything before 11:00.

| Time | What happens |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive **B**, unload until 09:05 ✓ done before 09:30 opening |
| 09:05 | Drive to A (25 min) |
| 09:30 | Arrive **A**, unload until 09:45 ✓ within 09:00–10:00 window |
| 09:45 | Drive to C (40 min) |
| 10:25 | Arrive near **C**, **30-minute break** until 10:55 ✓ uses the wait |
| 11:00 | Unload at **C** until 11:15 ✓ not before 11:00 |
| 11:15 | Drive to depot (45 min) |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot**, with no time to spare |

**The return has no slack at all.** C can't start before 11:00, and unloading plus the drive back takes exactly 60 minutes. Leaving earlier doesn't help, so a slow unload or any traffic after 11:00 makes him late. Ways to buy margin:
- Ask office C whether it can accept from 10:30 or 10:45. The driver is waiting nearby anyway.
- Check whether "back by 12:00" is a hard limit, and what happens if he's ten minutes late.
- Make sure C's items are loaded so they come off quickly.

## Van name ideas

- **Vincent Van Go**
- **The Dovetail Express**
- **Polly Ethylene**
- **The Restorer Rover**
- **Chester Drawers**

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> Hi [Name], our driver is on the way with your furniture and should be with you in about [20] minutes. See you soon!

## Three checks before handing over furniture

1. **Condition:** look for scratches, dents or chips from the journey, especially on corners and edges. Photograph each piece once it's in place.
2. **Function:** drawers slide, doors open and close properly, the piece sits level, and nothing wobbles.
3. **Completeness:** keys, shelves, handles, fixings and any loose parts are all there.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Email, signed on a phone or tablet at the door.** It can't get lost, it carries the time automatically and can include photos, and the customer gets a copy straight away. Keep a few paper notes in the van in case the device or the signal fails.

## Proof of delivery, in one line

> **Proof of delivery** is the record, usually a signature, a timestamp and photos, showing that the customer received their item in good condition.

## Evening-before text (147 characters)

> Hi Sarah, your furniture from Oak & Grain is due tomorrow 10-11am. We'll text when the driver's on the way. Any questions, just reply here. Thanks!

A long customer or business name could push it over 160, so check the length for each customer. Avoid emojis and curly apostrophes as well: many phones then switch to a different character set, which cuts the single-message limit to 70 characters.
